The same consideration exactly applies to the supplementary war appropria-

tion measure. Both these measures relate to expenditures for the fiscal year that is past, not the current year.

speechtext:
I shall couple with my motion two undertakings for the protection of opposition parties in the house. Mr. Speaker, I move:
That the provision of standing order 28 relative to the consideration of estimates which have not been first taken up on any other day than Thursday or Friday be suspended on Thursday and Friday, the 3rd and 4th of April, 1941.
The reason why it is necessary to pass this motion is that in those supplementary estimates are votes for a number of departments which have not yet been taken up on Monday or Tuesday of any week during this session.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, April 2, consideration in committee of Bill No. 25, for granting to His Majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley- Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 2-Appropriation.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a few questions I should like to ask in connection with these vast expenditures of money. Some days ago I referred to the
fact that the report of the auditor general did not give particulars of expenditures below $5,000. If a man has several contracts for less than $5,000, or for $4,999.99, no particulars of those contracts will appear in the public accounts. I do not agree with that system. If the electors of this countiy want complete information about expenditures, and members of parliament are unable to supply that information from official publications, then it seems to me our present system is not fair to the electors who are entitled to information. The answer will probably be given that the Department of Munitions and Supply is furnishing monthly statements which give the names of persons, firms or companies which have received payments, and the amounts. For instance, these monthly statements will show payments to Swifts, to Canada Packers and to many other corporations. But this is not satisfactory information. It takes up a lot of space, but no hon. member can tell from the information how much money has been paid, say in six months, to Swifts, to Canada Packers, to the Dominion Steel corporation or to any other corporation or individual. A member of parliament would have to be an adding machine to know all the amounts paid to these corporations or individuals.
Even to supply members of parliament with the amounts paid would still not be satisfactory, because we would not know for what the payments had been made. Take Swifts and Canada Packers as an example. We know that they sell bacon, ham, beef, perhaps vegetables and many other items, and we should be told why money has been paid to them. It is not enough simply to know that such an amount has been paid to a certain firm; we should be told why it has been paid. The only way an hon. member can understand what has happened is to know the quantity of meat or food or clothing or munitions which has been bought from each firm or individual during a certain period. But that still is not enough information for hon. members. We should be told how many soldiers have been fed with that food. We should be told the price per pound in order that we may see if there is extravagance or graft.
We have nothing of that kind. I have a whole library of publications in my room but they mean nothing. I defy the minister to give me the information I asked for. That is the only way we can have a full understanding of the matter. There is no hon. member who would be crazy enough to take this library of books and play the role of an adding machine in order to get information.

2122	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
Once there was a great mathematician who used to solve the most difficult problems. One day someone gave him a problem. There was a ship 515 feet long, 55 feet wide and with a depth of 16 feet; it had on board
9,000	tons of merchandise; there were 356 passengers, a crew of 125 men and 25 officers; the vessel had three masts, three funnels, two anchors and two propellers-what was the age of the captain? The mathematician worked on that problem for three days and finally found that the age of the captain was 56 years, 10 months, three days, six hours and ten minutes at the moment he dropped his pencil. It is not possible for members of parliament to make such calculations from the information we have. I do not pretend to be a good enough mathematician to discover the age of the captain from the information supplied to us monthly.
I do not say this in a critical way; I offer it as constructive criticism. For what was this money paid? We are not here to pass legislation, although there are a few bills on the order paper. Everything is being done by order in council by virtue of the War Measures Act. We are informed of what has been done six months after it has been done. We are here simply to vote subsidies, and in order to do that intelligently we should have the right kind of information. We are given what is supposed to be information, but what is only a mass of figures that run together. No one can use them to make intelligent comparisons or to obtain necessary information. How many soldiers are being fed with this food? How many soldiers are being equipped with this equipment? How many soldiers are being supplied with this ammunition, and what is the ammunition? These are not secrets of war. Since we have had no secret sessions I do not see why we cannot discuss these matters in the house.
I suggest to the government that they should change completely their method of giving out information. Instead of supplying us with large books containing information which is impossible to digest, we should be given statements that will convey real information to us and put us in a position to defend the policy of the government. What interest is it to the electors of any constituency to know that so much money has been paid each week to Swifts or to any other company? The people are not interested in that. They want to know how our soldiers are being fed, how they are being equipped, how they are being armed. I do not belong to that legion of superiores and sapientes which has invaded Ottawa. I am just a plain man who wants some information and who wants to be able

to vote intelligently upon these expenditures of money.
There is another thing which is equally interesting. What amount of the money that has already been spent since the beginning of the war has been spent in Canada for the defence of Canada, and how much has been spent in England for the defence of England? That is a fair question. There are, of course, two schools of thought, one proclaiming that the defence of England is the defence of Canada, and the other proclaiming that the defence of Canada is the defence of Canada alone. These are two divergent views and I respect them both. But as representatives of the taxpayers we are interested in knowing how much money has been spent here for the defence of Canada, and how much money has been spent over there or in Canada for the defence of Great Britain. This is a question that any elector may ask of any one of us, and whether you are an imperialist or not you are bound to give an immediate answer. But we cannot obtain that information from the public accounts, and I regret that my hon. friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply is unable to answer that question, because the figures are not disclosed in such a way that even the minister himself could be informed on that question.
I want a hierarchy in each department, and I want a hierarchy in the government. My view is that the Prime Minister of Canada is the boss of this country and that each one of his ministers should be boss in his own department. So long as that condition obtains I am all for it.
But there is something else. It is not necessary to be an expert to study the tabulations and charts which have been furnished to us. I notice, of course, that there have been some changes in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I am not in a position to say whether they are for the better or the worse, but evidently what was done in the first place was not perfect because it has been changed. What has been changed may now be perfect, but I am not quite sure about that. We will see what happens later on. My remarks are made in a friendly spirit.
I have here two charts of the Department of Munitions and Supply. One of them, dated November, 1940, appeared in a periodical published in the queen city of Toronto, and the other was put on Hansard by the minister on February 26 last. A comparison shows that there have been some changes. In the first place Mr. Gordon Scott was financial adviser. After his untimely death he was not replaced. There is no longer any financial adviser. On the other hand there was a Mr. Aubrey Davis, who was technical

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
consultant on leather. He has since been promoted as special adviser to the minister. I wonder why Mr. Gordon Scott has not been replaced by another gentleman as financial adviser.
There are many other things I could mention, but I shall mention only one after a short preamble. The members of the house who sat here from 1935 to 1940 must remember that I protested vehemently when the power of purchase was taken from the Minister of National Defence and transferred to the Minister of Finance. I opposed it for the same reason that I opposed the policy respecting the comptroller of the treasury. It was altogether too much for the Minister of Finance to make the purchases required for national defence, and in fact for a time the Minister of National Defence was unable to purchase even a cap for a soldier or a can of bully beef or anything else because he was not responsible for payment for these purchases. As my hon. friends know who are in the legal profession or in business, no commercial transaction is completed unless there is a payment specified and authorized by one of the contracting parties. Therefore the whole matter of purchases with regard to national defence wras for a certain time put under the Minister of Finance, and it was a real scandal. Some day I shall tell the house all the reasons why I objected so strongly. Finally, when the present Minister of National Defence became Minister of Finance he realized the absurdity of the whole thing, and shortly afterw'ards the defence purchasing board became the Department of Munitions and Supply, with a minister in charge.
That is all right. I have often advocated in this house that we should have ministers in charge of purchases for the war departments. The raison d'etre of the department of munitions was precisely those purchases and the manufacture of munitions under the authority of a minister of munitions, a power which before was under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defence.
But when I turn to look at the most recent chart of February 26, I see that purchases are now made in a very different way. There is a purchasing branch. There are two directors general; a director, Mr. John Eaton, and a general purchasing agent; and there are divisions corresponding to a certain extent with the divisions for the production branch of the department of munitions. In law, one of the most interesting matters is the study of comparative legislation; and of course we must proceed by comparison to understand anything in the charts which are submitted to us.
14873-134}
There is shown, at the left, the munitions production branch; then there is shown the aircraft production branch. In the middle is shown the purchasing branch for all materials which the department is not manufacturing itself and which are to be supplied through the Department of National Defence.
I shall not at present discuss the production branch. I shall deal only with the purchasing branch, which is divided into: barrack stores; building and office supplies; clothing, foodstuffs; fuels, paints, lubricants, electrical supplies; government and controlled companies; mechanical tools and hardware; mechanical transport; medical and dental supplies; miscellaneous militia and naval stores. Those are the divisions of the branch. Besides there are the local purchasing offices.
Hon. members may be under the impression that all purchases are made by that branch. We have, however, representatives abroad who are responsible, not to that purchasing branch, but to the deputy minister. We have overseas accounting which is in the comptroller's branch, which has not-on the chart-to do with representatives abroad. I cannot see why the overseas accounting should not be on the chart with the representatives abroad; it is the same thing.
There is something else. In order to be fair to the gentlemen who are in charge of the purchasing branch of the department, all purchases should be made by them. There should be a hierarchy of that branch; the subchiefs should be responsible to Mr. Price, Mr. Price should be responsible to Mr. Eaton, and Mr. Eaton should be responsible to Mr. Gagnon and Mr. Malkin. Well, it is not so, according to that chart, and this seems to me to be fundamentally wrong. But there is more to it. Some other corporations have been consti-tituted to make particular purchases independently of the purchasing branch. They are not responsible to the purchasing branch; they are responsible also to the deputy minister.
These government-owned companies are: Allied War Supplies Corporation; Citadel Merchandising Company, Limited; Fairmont Company, Limited; Federal Aircraft, Limited; Research Enterprises, Limited; Small Arms, Limited; and two new ones, Melbourne Merchandising, Limited, and Plateau Company, Limited. Later on I may show the business connection which exists between these men,-the ordinary business connections of these men whom we are asked to believe are supermen and in a position to handle this business better than anyone else. Well, there is one thing we all know. It is that these people, although they may be public-spirited to a certain extent, have been working until the war, and legitimately so, for personal gain. And this is not an attack, it is just an observation based on knowledge of human nature. No one can blame a man who is in business for trying to succeed as well as he can and to make personal gains which are legitimate. But the question is here. There are those who make real sacrifices for this country. Immediately behind those who are in the theatre of war are the politicians with the right spirit, who, very often, have to sacrifice their own personal interest to do the right thing, to serve their people aright, and to represent them as they are worthy to be represented.
Without casting aspersions on anyone, do you think, sir, that the amalgamation of personal interests can be mysteriously changed into public spirit? It is hard to say. Of course, we must consider human nature as it is; and if we are sitting here now it is because our constituents at the last election gave us a mandate, and the checking of public expenditures is something that we do in our capacity as members of parliament. Therefore we are entitled to all information. Members of the House of Commons ought not to be regarded as country cousins. I have said that once before and I repeat it. Although no one of us of the rank and file pretends to be gifted with superior qualities, we can all claim to be at least of the average, otherwise thousands of people would not have voted for us in the last election. When I say that I pay a compliment not only to my Liberal friends but also to the leader of the opposition and his supporters, to the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth group and his supporters and to the leader of the Social Credit group and his supporters. It is a compliment I pay to all.
It is said that there is more wisdom in two heads than in one. How much more wisdom,

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
therefore, should there be in 229 heads than in 16? I should like to have some information from the minister about the regulations with respect to these government-owned companies. We know only that a company has been formed and certain gentlemen are in it. What are the regulations with respect to these companies, and why is it that the purchases have to be made by these people? I find it very strange. There is a good deal of mystery, particularly about the Allied War Supplies Corporation, and I am not the first one to notice it. The Ottawa Journal said so last year and wanted some information, and I have asked for a bit of information. But now that that company supervises the chemical and explosives programme I want to know more about it. I have expressed my views and made a few suggestions, and I have asked some questions. There are many liaison officers in the department. What are their particular duties? I do not say that in a purely critical mood; I say it by way of constructive criticism, for two reasons-so that members may have intelligible information given to them, and so that there can be a check upon foolish expenditure, or expenditure that is not for the real purpose of the war, but just to enrich a few. Such information would give members an opportunity to check what is being done and might prevent scandal and great embarrassment to the ministry. I notice that since I have been speaking the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) has been sitting on our side, but I do not know whether he would be accepted by the party.

speechtext: It is because the hon. member quit that I came back.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I hesitate to take up the time of the committee, but there is a matter which I believe should be discussed under paragraph (c) of section 2, which reads:
(c) promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever.
Men everywhere are speaking of the need of cutting down our wheat acreage. Why? Because we cannot use our wheat production. We must stop growing wheat and start growing something else. But what shall that something else be? That is the question, and the answer no one seems to know.
Word has now come from Alberta that Canadian Sugar Factories Limited, with plants at Raymond and Picture Butte, have demanded a reduction of 1,300 acres in the sugar beet acreage in Alberta for 1941. The company says it has 200.000 hundredweight of sugar
unsold; and yet Canadians in 1939 consumed
1,163,000,000 pounds of sugar! Of that amount only one-eighth was beet sugar!
Why should Canada not devote more acres to the production of sugar? This question must arise in every normal mind. People should exact a most searching, candid and minute answer from every minister in the government who is in any way concerned with the question.
Canada is raising each year about three times as much wheat as she can consume. She is storing it. Why should Canada not produce twice as much sugar each year as she is able to consume, and store it? Why is it that this question has not occurred to more people in the country? Sugar to Canadians seems one of the absolute necessities of life. Sugar will keep in Canada for a long time. Sugar can be produced in Canada cheaply, surely, plentifully, and in every way profitably to Canadians. In the name of common sense, why not?
To decrease our wheat acreage, a good method would be to increase our sugar beet acreage.
During the last few years Canadian total consumption of all sugar and Canadian total production of beet sugar have been as follows:

To get a true picture of the beet sugar industry as a potential means of relief to our wheat problem, I point out that at least

The 300,000 acres of beets would have yielded the government during this last year, if we had been raising our own beet sugar, $52 an acre in revenue, which would amount to $15,600,000. It would, moreover, have saved the government 70 cents on each bushel of twenty bushels to the acre, at least, on

Some may ask, how do we estimate the amount of land necessary to produce the sugar that Canada would require? Eight per cent of Canada's 1940 estimated consumption

Now 93,466,400 pounds is approximately eight per cent of Canada's estimated 1940 consumption of 1,155,000,000 pounds. To produce all of Canada's supply on land as good, and under conditions as favourable, as obtained in the Lethbridge area last year, would require 300,000 acres of beets.
What amount of land would have been removed from the production of wheat? How do we compute that? The total amount of land diverted from wheat or other production by the use of this 300,000 acres for sugar beets I arrive at as follows. Mr. Russell in the above-mentioned letter says:
Every acre seeded to sugar beets will take at least ten acres out of wheat with a revenue to the government of at least $52 per acre from every acre seeded to beets.
Computing from these figures, we find that to raise the 300,000 acres of beets would take out of wheat production in Canada ten times
300,000	or 3,000,000 acres. This land would be the choicest of land. Upon it would normally be raised at least thirty to thirty-five bushels of wheat an acre.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does the growing of beets on the land take more strength from it than the growing of wheat, or does it benefit the land?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Growing of beets
greatly improves the land. In the first place, there are, on the beets, numerous little roots *which, when the beets are pulled, are left in the ground. These little roots tend to enrich the soil. Then, again, the beets strike roots deep into the soil, opening it up and admitting the air, this again greatly improving the friability of the soil.
Estimating the wheat yield on our ten times 300,000 acres at only twenty bushels to the acre, so as to be very conservative, we arrive at twenty times 3,000,000, or 60,000,000 bushels of wheat. That much less wheat to worry about should be a considerable relief to the government.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Could we use all the sugar?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am talking on the basis of Canada's sugar consumption. I pointed out that Canada consumes as much sugar as, on the basis of Canada's 1940 consumption, it would take 300,000 acres of beet land a year to produce.

Suppose Canada began to raise her sugar to some such extent as she is raising wheat, and stored the sugar against an evil day, which might easily come. If I might break in here just to say a word to the government, I would say I believe that as a government and as a people we are altogether too lethargic, altogether too self-assured; we assume that because things always have been all right, they are going to continue to be so. What would be the condition if German sea-raiders should get abroad upon the seas to the extent that they were able to destroy the ships that bring our sugar to Canada? There are other things which could occur in Canada which would destroy our present sources of sugar. Would the government not feel altogether blameworthy if it were found, in an emergency of that sort, that there was no sugar in the bowl, no sugar in the bin, and the people of Canada were without sugar? That is quite possible. We take great satisfaction in the fact that we have all this wheat as an assurance against future contingencies; we should be just as glad to have a similar store of sugar; for sugar is almost as near to being a basic necessity as wheat.
I proceed. Should Canada decide, in order to build up a reserve, to raise twice as much sugar as is required to supply her needs for a year, she could reduce her wheat production between 100 and 120 million bushels a year, at a conservative estimate. But, someone will object, the cost of buying and storing the sugar, as we now buy and store wheat, might be prohibitive. Let us turn to that matter for a moment or two. On the 1937 refiners' price basis of $4-006 per hundred, the cost of buying a year's sugar supply would be about $46,200,000 in a year. I multiply by four the 1,155,000,000 pounds which Canada consumed in 1940. Roughly, that is the means of making the computation. We arrive, then, at about $46,000,000 a year to provide Canada complete security with respect to sugar in that year. Storage could be provided at the factories in much the same way as we now provide extra storage at elevators for wheat.
To decrease our wheat acreage, our potential wheat carryover and our wheat storage problem ; to build up a productive machine to provide our sugar supply; and to collect a safe sugar reserve, must surely offer a most attractive prospect to any loyal Canadian who is really interested in Canada's welfare.
Blessed is the nation that does not have to buy abroad. Blessed is the nation that can produce its needs of wheat, sugar, coal, wool, fruits and vegetables, lumber, and animal products. Hon. members will note that in that list the ones of which we do not produce

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
adequate supplies are sugar and wool. Such a nation can be rich and economically free, much as a farmer on a good, mixed, well equipped farm can be economically free.
John Maynard Keynes is reported to have said recently:
Do not be deceived by the bogy of finance. It is no longer what it was. To-day it rears only a timid head. That is not the way it behaved in 1918 and 1919. In post-war reconstruction it is the physical things that will matter most, our man-power and our will-power and our capacity to have the necessary materials. We must go ahead on the basis of the physical realities of the situation.
If that means anything for Canada, it means surely that Canada should provide herself with the means of producing her sugar supply. Lord Balfour, acting as chairman of the meeting at which John Maynard Keynes is reported to have made those observations, is reported to have said that it was-
-like a breath of fresh air to hear Mr. Keynes speak on finance as he did that day.
He was speaking at the housing centre in London, and the excerpt is reported in the Ottawa Citizen of March 26, 1941.
Surely an attractive prospect is possible for Canada; but Canada thus far has chosen to turn aside from the path to such an obviously sound objective. Her sugar beet acreage has been reduced 1,300 acres for 1941. Let us reflect for a moment upon the loss of finance and income she is to sustain by this ill-advised move. Let us study the meaning of these 1,300 acres of beets to the Canadian government.
What will that move cost the federal government in direct outlay? Those 1,300 acres will go into wheat on prepared, choice land, and will yield at least 35 bushels to the acre. This is in the Lethbridge area, where the record at the experimental farm respecting wheat produced on irrigated land for twenty-seven years has been an average of 52-8 bushels to the acre on one plot and 40-8 bushels on another.
The result will be that there will be produced on that land 45,500 bushels, which the federal government will be called upon to pay for at the rate of 70 cents a bushel, costing that government $31,850 in hard cash. That is the first payment we must make.
By next year there will be ten times 1,300 acres going back into wheat. One-half at least of the 13,000 acres, (the result of multiplying 1,300 by ten) or 6,500 acres will be planted to wheat, yielding 35 bushels to the acre, totalling 227,500 bushels. That quantity, at 70 cents a bushel, will total $159,250
the government will have to pay in 1942. That amount would buy a good many Spitfires.
In addition to that, the government will lose revenue estimated at 1,300 times $52, or $67,600. Besides that, it will lose its income tax and sales tax. It will lose the war savings people would have bought, and the revenues derived from tariffs on goods people in that area would have bought. When the computation is made, I believe the government will find that it is a good deal worse off because somebody blundered over sugar last year.
What will be the cost of that manoeuvre to the farmers and to the people generally? In the first place, there will be a loss of beets. We find that 1,300 acres yielding 14-10 tons to the acre-the 1940 yield-would amount to 18,330 tons. That amount, valued at $6.69 a ton, the 1938 price-and it will be noticed that I am attempting to produce the figures for years before the war-would bring about $122,627.70. This means that in 1941 there will be taken from the hands of the people who might buy war savings certificates an amount of $122,627.70, which might have been derived from beets alone in the Lethbridge federal riding.
In addition to beets there would be by-products-beet	tops, beet pulp and
molasses-equivalent to the meat-producing value of 1,300 acres of corn. The ordinary member of the house indicates quite clearly by his attitude while I am talking that he does not even dream of the possibility of the beet industry in Canada. It has not dawned on hon. members that the value of the by-products alone from an acre of beets is as great in the production of meat as is the value of an acre of corn, a product which has made so many states in the United States wealthy.
The beets, beet tops, molasses and pulp from 1,300 acres of beets will be lost to the people of Canada. Beet tops alone, when fed to lambs in an experiment extending over three years in Wyoming and Montana, where they are using a little better sense than we are using in Canada, were found to be valued at $1.30 for every ton of beets. That, again, is a complete loss right at a time when the mother country needs meats of various kinds.
The loss of sugar on the 1,300 acres, if we figure a yield of fourteen tons to the acre, which is a little less than last year, will amount to 18,200 tons. With a yield of 306 pounds of sugar per ton, which yield was obtained in 1939, this would represent 5,569,200 pounds of sugar. Taking a price of $6.15, which
2128	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
was the price prevailing on March 29 before the government so ill-advisedly raised it, this would amount to $342,505.80.
In addition, as a result of this move, markets will be lost for certain raw materials. In the case of coal this would be worth $6,111. This would be all-Canadian coal, not coal brought in from Pennsylvania. In the case of lime rock the lost market would be $2,222. This also is a Canadian product. In the case of coke the value would be $1,000; boxes, et cetera, $11,666; bags and other essentials, $11,111; freight, $36,666, and labour, $19,444. That is the amount of the payroll of the men who would work in the factory processing the product of these 1,300 acres. Payments to growers and farmers would be $104,444. The figures I am giving are based upon statistics which will be found on page 15 of "Why Canada Needs Sugar Beets."
In addition, there will be lost in that area sales of clothing, shoes and other products cf eastern manufacturers to an amount which no one can conceive.
A still further loss is the'soil improvement which would come by way of increased fertility, increased fibre and increased tilth, as I indicated in my answer to the hon. member for Davenport.
As a result of this move, there will be fed in the Lethbridge riding 2,000 fewer sheep and 500 fewer cattle in the coming year, a year when we shall be needing sheep and cattle produced in the west.
What will be the cost to the Canadian economy? First, there will be increased unemployment; second, there will be less real wealth; third, there will be less price stability. May I stop for a moment to point out once more, as I have done scores of times in this house, that the cause of inflation in a country is the decrease of goods. This move will decrease goods in Canada, and therefore, will endanger the stability of our dollar and will be risking inflation. Fourth, there will be less economic security; fifth, less economic freedom and independence, and, sixth, less effectiveness in the war. These will be the effects upon our Canadian economy. In the case of 1,300 acres they may not be serious, but in the case of 13,000 acres they would be quite serious, in the light of conditions during and after the war.
Who is responsible for this magnificent achievement? He has small cause for pride. He has achieved something that will long stand to his shame. In the first place, the responsibility must rest upon the sugar controller; next, upon the war-time prices and trade board and, next, upon whoever gives
[Mr. BlackmoreJ
them orders: first, in the government; second, through the government and, third, outside the government In order to show that what I am saying is based upon good evidence, I should like to read from order in council P.C. 1983. I quote:
All sugar refiners in Canada shall sell to the sugar administrator as and when required by him, all raw sugar, and all refined sugar, syrups, liquid sugar and molasses manufactured from beet or cane now or hereafter in their possession at such prices as the sugar administrator, under the direction of the war-time prices and trade board, from time to time may prescribe and, to effectuate such power, the sugar administrator, under the direction of the board, shall have power to take possession of all or any such sugars accordingly.
I think the wording of that passage places responsibility directly upon the shoulders of the sugar administrator and the war-time prices and trade board. If they have received instructions from someone else, I believe they are entitled to have the Minister of Labour tell us about it when he gives his statement on sugar. I do not think it is quite fair to let people like them bear the odium of such a mischievous manoeuvre.
What can be the reason for this move to reduce this acreage by 1,300 acres at a time like this? Is it done in order that we may have cheaper prices in Canada? That seemed to be the idea conveyed in the minister's vague expressions we heard in the house the other day. If the move was designed to bring about cheaper prices in Canada, will someone tell me why there have been so many increases in the price of sugar since the war broke out? Why was there an increase of 35 cents on May 20, 1940? It might be said that this was brought about by the sugar administrator of Great Britain; I shall have more to say about that later on. Evidently the object of this scheming in Canada is not to make prices lower for the Canadian people. If it were, why the excise taxes by which the Liberal government has taken away from the people of Canada a total of $11,000,000 during every year of Liberal administration? It has taken it away from the poorest people. The tax is inevitable; everyone must pay. The suffering returned soldier getting $8 a month by way of pension has to pay his share, almost as great a share as that of the fortunate millionaire. Yet we have been talking about equality of sacrifice in this country!
Was this move made in order to ensure a stable supply of sugar? That was the next hint conveyed by the vague expressions the other day. If it was designed to ensure stable supplies, then why this move in the direction of placing Canada at the mercy of a group of bankers and big interests, of outsiders and foreigners who control, directly or

Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
indirectly, the sugar establishments in the great sugar producing areas from which Canada is being made to draw her cane supplies? A real stability of sugar supplies for Canada lies in the establishment of a beet sugar industry. Let the government expend
835,000,000 in building factories of 1,600 ton slicing capacity in Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, British Columbia and Alberta as a war measure. In ten years those factories, without exorbitant prices being charged, will all be paid for out of the profits, and there will be established in Canada a splendid stability, a source of wealth, security, power, financial integrity, good homes, population, prosperity, happiness and independence.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: May I ask, for information, whether as high a grade of sugar can be made from sugar beets as from cane sugar?

speechtext: Yes. I went into that at length and with great care in my speech in this house on June 26, last year, and the hon. member will find in Hansard of that date that the evidence is conclusive that beet sugar is in every sense a complete equivalent of cane sugar.

Would such a proposition be a sound one for the government? The government is investing huge amounts of money in munitions plants and, before the war is much older, will be investing a great amount of money in homes, and in so doing, the dominion government are taking a highly commendable step. It is completely right that they should do so. To invest money in beet sugar factories would be to insure not only Canada's war supply of sugar but, as well, her post-war supply.
We can gather an idea of the soundness of the proposal from the record of the Raymond sugar factory in my constituency. It was established in 1925, when wheat prices were high, in the period called the "roaring twenties" in the United States, when not only wheat prices but prices of labour to harvest and handle wheat were high. It was an exceedingly difficult time in which to get people to plant and to handle beets cheaply enough to enable the producers to make a profit sufficient to carry on; but the Raymond sugar factory came serenely through those trying years, notwithstanding the fact that in 1928 in the early days of October a most unprecedented mishap occurred, a very severe frost which froze the
beets into the ground and caused a tremendous loss to the sugar factories. Notwithstanding that, the Raymond sugar factory rode triumphant through the storm. speechtext:
The hon. member for Medicine Hat was kind enough to give me a few moments before he addressed the committee.
I do not intend to enter to-day into any debate on the problem of sugar. I wish to refer to only one statement that was made by the hon. member for Lethbridge. Most of his address has more reference to the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance than to the war-time prices and trade board. In connection, however, with the question of why a wider expansion of the sugar beet industry was not taking place, he cited as a primary cause the passing of order in council P.C. 1983. That order in council provides that all sugar refineries in Canada shall sell to the sugar administrator, as and when required by him, all raw sugar, et cetera; I shall not take up the time of the committee to read the whole paragraph. The hon. member has entirely misconceived the purpose for which that order in council was passed. It was passed for one specific purpose which has nothing to do with a limitation of sugar beet acreage.
At the time it became apparent that, in accordance with our dealings with the British sugar controller, there would be an increased price of sugar. It was well known that if that fact became widespread, the price of sugar would assuredly rise, that is both the retail and the wholesale prices, with the inevitable result that the refineries would make large inventory profits to which it was felt they were not entitled. The order in council had nothing to do with a limitation of sugar beet acreage. It had nothing whatever to do with any other purpose than that for which it was specifically passed. In order to avoid these profits on sugar which had heretofore been sold by the administrator to the refineries, it was provided that the administrator would repurchase that sugar at the
2132	COMMONS
Supplementary IFur Appropriation Bill
prices at which he had sold it to the refineries, and would immediately thereafter resell it to the refineries at the enhanced price. In other words, it was simply a method of giving to the government and the people of Canada the inventory rise which, in the normal course, would otherwise have accrued to the refineries.
I do not think there is in the hon. member's speech another point to which I need now refer. No doubt an occasion will arise when we shall have a more appropriate opportunity of debating the sugar question, and at that time I shall be glad to participate.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I shall be extremely
brief, but I do realize that the matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Lethbridge is one of urgency and extreme importance in a large part of this country.
We find that, in England, some 22 per cent of the sugar is made from home-grown material; in the United States, 25 per cent; whereas in Canada it is only 12-40 per cent. Furthermore, we find that the refiners are reducing and forcing the growers to reduce their sugar beet acreage. This is going to have a disastrous effect upon the economy of the people of that district. This is an industry which would help in some measure to bring up the income of agriculture, because figures have been produced in this house to show that the agricultural population of the country are not getting their share of the national income at the present time.
We have irrigation districts and there is great need for development of more irrigation. In years gone by, irrigation systems have been started and not completed, and in order to produce more sugar beets to balance our economy, if these irrigation districts could be completed a great benefit would result. With regard to the cattle industry, this government was fortunate enough to make an agreement with the United States-and the government deserves credit for it-whereby we are allowed a generous quota in the United States markets at half the previous rate of duty. We are not, however, altogether filling that quota, and the encouragement of the beet sugar industry would help the cattle industry through the use of tops, pulp, molasses and other by-products. A great benefit could be derived from this source.
In recent years the great unemployment menace was one of the worst things that struck this and other countries. Producing sugar from home grown raw material would provide employment for twenty times the number of people for whom producing the same amount of sugar from imported cane

would provide employment. That is one big factor. Again, it has been rumoured and hinted that there in the near future will be a tax on sugar. I would appeal to the Minister of Finance so to regulate that tax that it will bear less heavily upon sugar produced from home-grown raw materials. I believe that, if the tax could be adjusted in that way, great benefit would result.
Someone has questioned the quality of beet sugar. I am quite sure that it compares favourably with that of cane sugar; it conforms exactly to the same chemical formula, and the people who are using it do not object to it. The prejudice against it is dying out and, under modem methods of manufacture, it is exactly the same as cane sugar.
We are engaged in a war of such magnitude that the very foundations of the temple of liberty and freedom are being threatened. We know that the months ahead may be dark, but beyond those months there are surely brighter things coming, and we hope that there will be a more ample life, more equality of opportunity, and better home conditions.
It has been said, and said by the Prime Minister, that we look for a new order to replace the old order; but if we wait until the war is over for that new order to come, we shall look in vain for it. It must be planned and prepared for and worked on. It cannot be reduced to writing at a conference, and so in preparing for the great rehabilitation problem which will face this country, some of the things I have mentioned will be of great value-irrigation schemes to provide homes, security for the people in those homes, and the encouragement of the beet sugar industry, the sheep industry, the cattle industry, to balance our economy and provide employment for those who will be released from war activities and for the strangers who will come to our land at that time.

When the house rose last evening, I was out of the chamber for a few moments, but on looking over Hansard to-day I find that the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), in concluding his observations just prior to the adjournment, made the following statement with reference to the contribution that I had made to the debate. I wish to correct the impression he left. As reported at page 2114 of Hansard, he said:
It is entirely wrong to endeavour to create the impression, as set forth by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, that the Nova Scotia builders are saboteurs.

Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury):	He did not
say that.
Mr. Macdonald (Kingston City):	Yes, he
said that. He said they could be considered either as saboteurs or profiteers, because either they were reluctant to help the war effort or they wanted to make too much money.
With regard to what I did say, I will let Hansard speak for itself. I will quote the reference I made on that particular point, as reported at page 2102 of Hansard'.
I was disappointed also at the statement made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs, when he attempted to analyse the reason why shipbuilding has not been carried on more extensively in Nova Scotia. He pointed out that at one time shipbuilding was the major industry of this province. He said also that shipbuilding yards in Nova Scotia had been asked to tender, but that very few had even put in tenders, and those who did were twenty-five per cent higher in their prices than shipbuilding yards in other parts of Canada. He could give no reasonable explanation for this. The minister's statement amounted virtually to an accusation against the shipbuilders of Nova Scotia of sabotage or an attempt to obtain greater profits than other shipbuilders. In the light of the present situation I think that is a serious statement to make.
Personally I do not believe that any such thing is true.
I proceeded to elaborate on what I thought were the real reasons why shipyards in Nova Scotia were not able to compete with shipyards in other parts of Canada. Perhaps the minister misunderstood, in listening to the debate, exactly what I said. At any rate, I regard his remarks on that particular point as a misrepresentation of what I did actually say.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
On behalf of our group I support the representations that have been made by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw). I agree particularly with the hon. member for Medicine Hat, who said that we should be planning now for the after-war situation, and I am in thorough agreement with those who hold the view that the sugar beet industry of Canada is one that can be expanded to a very large degree during the war in order to save ship bottoms and supply our people with home grown sugar, transferring perhaps some of those who to-day are growing wheat and other commodities into a new line of production to meet the Canadian need. As has been shown by previous speakers, sugar beets would also provide valuable by-products. The by-products used for the feeding of cattle and so on are of material aid to the country at this time.
I do not wish to make a long speech; I think all that need be said in this matter is that we urge upon the government a reconsideration of the suggestion for acreage reduction in this regard; indeed, we go one step further and say that we believe the government should be giving every encouragement to the expansion of the sugar beet industry in Canada both as a war effort and as a valuable industry and asset to the country after the war.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think we should concur in the request made by the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Finance to put off this discussion until some future date, because I understand the, discussion this afternoon should not have taken place on this bill. I should, however, just like to say that it is not only Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario that are interested in the development of this industry; the province of Quebec is very much interested. I regret that more attention was not given by the government of Canada before to-day to this important industry in the interests of the farmer and also as something worth-while in the economics of Canada. I do not intend to take any more time at present, for the reason I gave at first, but I am pleased to note what the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour said, that we are going to have a further opportunity to discuss this problem of the beet sugar industry in Canada during the present session.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think I am now in order to continue my remarks. It will take me a very short time to finish, but there are a few things to be said which I consider important.
When my time expired I was discusing the soundness of the proposal that the dominion government should either invest $35,000,000 in first-class beet sugar refineries or cause other people to invest that amount in order that we should have production in Canada of a sufficient amount to enable all the sugar needs of Canada to be met from Canadian production. I had just cited the record of Canadian Sugar Factories Limited in 1937, which I think was a most excellent record.
There are other reasons why the proposal that the dominion should support the beet sugar industry is sound. The costs of production of beet sugar are falling rapidly, contrary to the commonly accepted idea. There is at the present time, I read, a machine invented by a man named Hardy in the United States which will enable a man and a boy with one machine to top five acres of beets a day. Anyone who knows anything about the cost of topping beets will realize that this will greatly reduce the cost of producing beet sugar.
2134	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
There is another machine which is described in the United States department of agriculture bulletin No. 488. This machine is designed to plant and block sugar beets much more cheaply. Then there are unusually fine machines being developed to unload and pile and handle sugar beets. All these dispense with labour and greatly speed up the process of making beet sugar and will unquestionably reduce the cost. Larger mills of 1,600 tons slicing capacity will cut down the unit overhead cost far below that possible for a 1,200 ton mill such as Raymond has. A longer campaign, say 120 days, will greatly decrease the cost of production, the overhead being much the same, and the number of days the factory runs being increased. The climate of Canada is especially adapted for a long run; in that respect being greatly superior to the climate of the main European sugar producing countries like Germany, Czechoslovakia and Roumania.
The explanation being given for this reduction of 1,300 acres is that it was brought about to help Britain win the war. It has been argued that the desire was to enable Canada to help to take the empire sugar supply. If that were the case, then will someone tell me why 200,000,000 pounds of sugar were imported in 1940 from Santo Domingo, 50,000,000 pounds from Cuba and 6,000,000 pounds from Haiti, all three non-British countries? And why were British ships used with the risk of shortage for Great Britain, and why was valuable foreign exchange which Canada could ill-afford spent for the buying of foreign sugar?
It is said that the reasons for this procedure are that the United Kingdom did not ration sugar until January, 1940; that the people, expecting rationing, bought heavily in Britain, and that during the last year the British West Indies crop was about 250,000 tons short and the Australian crop about 150,000 tons short. Every one of these is a reason why the sugar of the Raymond and Picture Butte factories should have been taken by the sugar administrator!
The Minister of Labour rose in his place in support of the administrator; I will ask him to deny this statement: that the sugar administrator is given control of everything pertaining to sugar in Canada, and could have taken the sugar from the Canadian sugar factories if he had so chosen. But he did not so choose.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He is under no obligation to take any definite amount of either preferential or full duty sugar whatever.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is, he has a perfectly free hand. That is to his condemnation, that, having a free hand, he neglected to

take the sugar off the hands of the Canadian sugar factories, thereby forcing them to cause their growers to reduce acreage by 1,300 acres in one year. The blame must be assumed either by that gentleman or by the war-time prices and trade board or by the men who gave them orders, whoever those men may be.
If Great Britain has to sell her sugar to Canada in order to pay for goods that she has to buy from Canada, if the price which Canada has to pay to help Britain is the destruction of the Canadian beet sugar industry, then I say that the British are asking too great a price from Canada. I do not believe the British asked it. That is not necessary. The dominion government could far better afford to give commodities to Great Britain to the amount that would be paid for by the sugar which Canada is buying from Great Britain than she can afford to take the sugar and deplete her own sugar producing resources.
The argument is sometimes advanced that Canada must trade. I challenge that statement. The big question is, can Canada be self-sufficient? If the reason why she must trade is that she cannot be self-sufficient, then why in the name of reason is it that sugar, which is a main item that prevents Canada from being self-sufficient, is the one item which is being sacrificed at the present time?
Also, why is someone in Canada managing matters in such a way that Canada is not producing the wool she needs, so that Canada has to import much of her wool from other countries when she is one of the best wool growing countries on the face of the earth? I use this just to show that it is not a sincere argument to say that Canada must inevitably trade. Canada, properly managed, does not have to trade. Canada is equipped by Providence to enable herself to live largely without having to trade with other people. And if we are going to be independent and economically free in this country, we must develop our potentialities.
We are importing a lot of com from abroad when we can raise corn here. We are importing coal when we can produce coal, oil when we can produce oil. The argument that Canada must inevitably trade is hypocrisy, Mr. Chairman. Canada can be self-sufficient, if certain overpowerful men in Canada will let her. Has Canada any insuperable necessity? If so, what is it? I will hear the answer, "Oh, rubber, citrus fruits, coffee, tea, bananas and so on." I freely grant all those, but-

That is all fine; I am glad to have them. But I ask you, Mr. Chairman, how in the name of common sense can we overcome our disability with respect to tin by putting ourselves under the disability of having to import sugar? That does not make sense.
Is the self-sufficiency policy unsound? I point to the United States and. her experience in the last war. When the last war came, the United States found herself unable to produce her own rubber. Greatly to her embarrassment she found herself unable to produce her own dyes, because she had been tricked into depending upon German sources for her dyes. The result was that the United States was in a most precarious position with respect to dyes. She was in the same position with respect to chemicals, and for the same reason. The United States was in a desperate condition with respect to sugar during the last war, because she had not got herself into the position where she could produce her own sugar.
May I read to the committee a statement in which I believe everyone would be interested. This comes from an article entitled "The Sugar Bowl is Mended", by Charles Morrow Wilson, and appears in the Country Gentleman for April, 1940. It contains words which have great significance for us at this time, and sets forth one of the reasons for my insisting upon debating this question at the present time. The article reads, in part:
When the first world war began Europe was growing almost enough sugar for its own use. But when the beet fields turned to battle fields Cuban production shot from 2,000,000 to more than 5,000.000 tons a year, and Cuba was sugar bowl for the world.
After the armistice tens of millions of war-rationed people were frantic for sweets, and sugar bins were empty. So in the early twenties Cuban sugar prices boomed to 24 cents per pound at the mills.
Mr. Chairman, it needs to be shown by the Minister of Labour, and by anyone else who is interested, whether or not the same gentlemen who were in charge of Cuba at that time are not in charge of Cuba to-day, and are not exercising a very strong influence over the British sugar control.

I happen to be somewhat familiar with this sugar question, I may tell the Minister of Labour. This is his first experience with me. Probably after a while he will realize that. It is sometimes argued that by increasing our importation of sugar from abroad we would increase our market for potatoes and salt fish from the maritime provinces. I have every sympathy with the maritimes; far be it from me to say anything which would jeopardize their position. But may I tell hon. members from the maritimes that in this respect they have been deluded. Much propaganda has been spread to confuse maritime minds. The arguments about potatoes and salt fish by such propagandists are devastatingly dealt with by Mr. Ralph P. Bell in an article of February 8, 1938 appearing in the Halifax Herald. I commend that article to hon. members from the maritimes. They will find that all this talk about sugar beet production impairing the position of the maritime salt-fish and potato markets is just pure piffle, and worse; it is sheer delusion.

speechtext:
From all the facts
I have set forth it would certainly appear, first, that the Canadian government is selling Canada into bondage in the matter of Canada's sugar supply.
Second, someone is bartering Canada's birthright for worse than a mess of pottage, betraying her future for dross as base as the famous thirty pieces of silver; for any nation that must buy from abroad any necessity of
2136	COMMONS
Supplementary War Appropriation Bill
life is, in respect of that necessity, a potential slave of external circumstances.
Third, the interests that control our sugar supply, once our beet sugar industry is destroyed, can raise the price to any level their unprincipled cupidity dictates, and, as they did after the last war, force Canadians to pay that figure.
Fourth, the sugar situation looms through the storm clouds as one of the blackest and most imminent threats to Canadian economic freedom.
The other day the Minister of Labour promised a statement in connection with the sugar situation. He will have to canvass the whole question carefully, for in his report he will have to show, first, why the Canadian beet sugar industry has been restricted in war time. He will find that a thorny question, and more thorny the more deeply he goes into it.
Second, why has Canada spent good exchange for foreign sugar, and left Canadian-grown sugar unused, with agriculture in the tragic condition in which it finds itself, and with a trade balance so dangerously against us, as it now is?
Third, why are prices of sugar rising, when raw cane can be bought for 75 cents per hundredweight in Haiti, Cuba, and Santo Domingo?
Fourth, why is the Canadian government apparently preparing to give Canada over to the spoilers who robbed her at the close of the last great war?
Fifth, why must Canada's consumer prices depend upon the will of the British sugar controller, when Canada could produce twice her needs at greatly reduced costs?
Sixth, while even the United States insists that 55-59 per cent of her domestic consumption shall be domestically produced, why can Canada afford to decrease even her meagre 12i per cent?
Seventh, who selected the present sugar controller? On whose instigation was the selection made, and why?
Eighth, is there not cause for grave suspicion that certain overpowerful Canadians are manipulating Canada's sugar supply to enrich themselves, to enslave Canadians and to exploit our people immeasurably?
The first question the ministers of Labour, Trade and Commerce, Agriculture, and Finance, and their colleagues need to answer is this: Do they intend to keep and to make Canada a free and independent democracy, or did Canadian unity in their election platform a year ago mean Canadian unity with the United States, or with the United States

and some other nation or nations? If the latter is the case, are they rendering such' unity unavoidable by policies tending to reduce Canada to economic helplessness? If they really desire a free Canada, then they must make her economically free. To do this, they must take steps to build up within Canada an adequate all-Canadian sugar supply. This they can do only by expanding the beet sugar industry.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the
questions asked by my hon. friend had to do with government-owned companies which he named. These companies operate just as any public company. They accept contracts from the government, execute them and carry out whatever duties are assigned to them by order in council, just as would any private business firm. In each case the treasurer of the company is an officer of the treasury branch of the government. The auditor of each company is an appointee of the auditor general of Canada. The procedure of these companies conforms to the best practice of corporations operating in this country.
The largest organization is the Allied War Supplies Corporation which deals with the explosives and chemical operations of the government. This company retains experts in the different branches of the work. Contracts are made with reputable contractors for the construction work involved, and in most instances contracts are made with the leading firms in the chemical and explosives business to operate plants on a management fee basis.
There are other companies, but I have told the house on several occasions that it is not desirable to elaborate on their operations too fully. These companies are doing the work of protecting the government against supplies of materials which come from foreign countries, and the sources of which may be subject to interruption from war causes. There is the Melbourne Merchandising Company Limited, the Plateau Company Limited, and one or two other commodity companies. These companies have the duty of making available supplies of such things as rubber, silk and other items, the names of which escape me at the moment. These companies operate just as any commodity company would. Purchases and sales are made, commodities are bought at the best market price obtainable and are sold at the current Canadian price. But in between the purchase and sale of commodities, considerable stocks are maintained to make sure that supplies will be available

Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the minister for what he has just said. However, referring to experts, I cannot see what particular experience Mr. Biggar has had. He may be a good lawyer, but I cannot understand what experience he would have in the manufacture of optical equipment. I should like to know what experience Mr. Dunning, who has been a trader, has had in supervising chemical and explosives manufacturing. I do not know what experience he has had in that respect, apart from being the understudy of that international Vulcan, Mr. Purvis. That is all there is in it. The minister must take what I say in the spirit in which I say it. I am simply trying to help him in his work, which I realize is quite heavy. He is, however, surrounded by a few men who think they can read before they learn their alphabet. They are somewhat like children who sometimes try to read upside down. The points I raised were not quite along the line of his answers.
There is one branch of the department-it does not matter whether you call it a branch or a division-which is responsible for purchases. In order that this branch should be treated fairly, they should have the entire responsibility; it should not be shared with another branch which is directly responsible to the deputy minister. These branches are asked to deal with all purchases of chemicals and so on. I shall read what the minister said and take this matter up with him privately in order to save the time of the committee. I would, however, remind the minister of one thing. We do not impute motives when we ask for information. We do this simply to satisfy those people who come to us for information, whether they live in or outside of our own constituencies.
I want to protect this purchasing branch. I do not wish to see them suffer by any encroachment on the part of these so-called companies. The Minister of Munitions and Supply is not a corporation lawyer, and I congratulate him. I think he will admit that most of the wrong which has been done in the
financial world has been done by corporation lawyers. Ninety-nine per cent of them are crooks. What are these blue-sky laws we hear about? What about the watered stock in these companies which have been organized by lawyers, who take a portion of it as their fee and retainers? Many companies have been ruined because of watered stocks, a large portion of which went into the pockets of the corporation lawyers.
I think it is all wrong to organize government business along corporation lines. You can go to any stock broker's office and look at the stocks, and see how people have been robbed through the formation of these companies. They do not offer a good example to be followed in government business. Any lawyer who knows the law and who knows the principles underlying our law will not do this sort of thing. Corporation practice in government is wrong. It is also wrong to canonize those who are part of the scheme, to make saints of them, to place halos upon their heads and then tell us that we must not criticize them. There is not a single item of information about expenditures that can properly be refused to members of parliament when we are sitting in committee like this. We are entitled to information about all expenditures. What should be secret?
There is no need for secrecy about the spending of public money. Secrecy is necessary about the plans by virtue of which certain kinds of arms and ammunition are being made and the places where they are being manufactured, and also as to war tactics. I want no information on these things because I admit they must be kept secret. But when it comes to the purchase of any kind of munitions, we must know how much is paid for them, and even if Hitler gets to know how much we pay for shells and guns and other munitions it will not endanger our position in the war. It might, however, embarrass some profiteers, and' we ought to embarrass them and prevent them from getting too much money from the public exchequer. This distinction should be made in determining what shall and what shall not be kept secret.
In the first place, no one in public business should be kept sacrosanct until after he is dead. So long as he is living and engaged in public business, he must be man enough to suffer criticism no matter where it comes from. In the second place, there should be no hiding place, no secrecy regarding public expenditures, which we are supposed to check in this house and not vote blindfold. I desire for a few moments to deal with a matter that is of considerable importance; otherwise I would not venture to delay the passage of the bill, which I regret has been delayed altogether too long.
Prior to 1931 the system of treasury control in this country was exceedingly inadequate. A system had grown up whereby parliament voted moneys, in the estimates or supplementary estimates, which were allocated to departments, but there was no treasury control of expenditures and frequently accounts were overdrawn. The situation became rather acute in 1931 with the fall of the national revenues during the depression. The government of

the day decided that the situation had to be grappled with and they introduced the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, which is to be found in chapter 27 of the statutes of 1931. I remember that bill very well. I had something to do with piloting it through the banking and commerce committee to which it was referred, and it was given thorough consideration by everyone and treated entirely in a businesslike manner. Section 29 of the act contains an important clause:
No contract, agreement, or undertaking of any nature, involving a charge on the consolidated revenue fund, shall be entered into, or have any force or effect, unless the comptroller-
That is, the comptroller of the treasury appointed under the authority of the act.
-or an officer of the Department of Finance designated by him and approved by the treasury board, shall have certified that there is a sufficient unencumbered balance available, out of the amount authorized by parliament for the particular service, to pay any commitments under such contract, agreement or undertaking which would, under the provisions thereof, come in course of payment during the fiscal year in which such contract, agreement or undertaking is made or entered into.
That was notice to these departments that the deputy ministers could not overdraw, and I remember that word went out at that time to the departments that any infraction of the law might call for the resignation of the deputy minister. That was the impression left on them, and a great evil was corrected.
At that time Mr. Watson Sellar, the present auditor general of Canada, was appointed comptroller of the treasury. He was appointed after the act was placed in the statutes by the Bennett government, and I was impressed, before the banking committee, with the knowledge he had of the proposed measure and the way it should work. I think that in every way he was an important official. He is now auditor general of Canada.
Recently I have been amazed to learn that by reason of the provisions of the War Appropriation Act 1940, which are similar to subsection 4 (1) (e) of the bill now before us, and presumably also from time to time under the authority of the War Measures Act, that provision of parliament has been set aside by the government by order in council, at times when this parliament was in session.
I challenge the position that the government has taken. I can readily understand that in a time of war a statute might be found too inflexible and that at a time when parliament was in recess it might be necessary-in fact,
I could imagine circumstances in which I think it would be absolutely necessary-that some extraordinary provision be taken to

cover any given commitment in war time. I suggest to the committee, however, that when parliament is in session, the setting aside by order in council of a statute of that kind, intended to be the safeguard of the public treasury, to protect the taxpayers of the country, is absolutely indefensible and cannot be justified on any ground of expediency or of war requirement or anything of the sort. If occasion is found when the provisions of the statute are too inflexible at a time when the House of Commons is in session, all the government have to do is to come to parliament and say so and explain the position, and power will be given to them. But to-day that is not the position. What has happened? An important section of the statutes of this country, intended to protect the public treasury, has been flouted by the minister, at a time when the people's representatives are in session and could correct the position if it absolutely needed to be corrected.

The Minister of Finance made it quite clear that only estimates could be made and that they would have to have wider powers. That seems surprisingly low, having regard to the rate at which we have been spending money. I am not making any observations with respect to what value we are getting for our money; I am only commenting on the rate at which we are spending money. I quote again:
That paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 5 of the War Appropriation Act, 1940, empowers the governor in council to make regulations prescribing administrative practices with respect to the making of financial commitments.
Paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 5 of last year's act was, I believe, identical with paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 4 of the bill now before us. On the basis of that statement contained in paragraph (e), which I have read more than once, His Excellency, the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, proceeds to change the law of this country while parliament is in session. I protest against any such practice, especially in connection with treasury expenditures and commitments. I quote again:
Now, therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, is pleased to make the following regulations regarding the making of financial commitments with respect to expenditures for war purposes, and they are hereby made and established accordingly:
1. War programmes shall, in the first instance, be submitted for the approval of the governor in council or the war committee and
any major changes in or additions to an approved programme shall also be submitted for the approval of the governor in council or the war committee. When submitting any original programme or changes in or additions to an approved programme the department concerned shall furnish in as much detail as is practicable at that time the information required under the next succeeding regulation.
On. the basis of that, the government of this country has gone ahead and altered the statute law of Canada. We have no longer any regard for the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. I admit at the very outset that in war time, when parliament is in recess, I can quite understand the necessity of having some additional authority. I question very much if the additional authority is to be found in paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of section 4, but it may be that the government has an opinion from the Department of Justice that they can do that.
This is what I want to put to the minister: If we still have responsible government in Canada, why should a government of this country override the laws of Canada by order in council, while parliament is in session, especially with respect to the expenditure of money? There is a great principle at stake here, the principle of parliamentary control and the supremacy of parliament. I never thought that I would live to see the day, even in war time, when a government led by my right hon. friend would take authority, under the flimsy pretext contained in that clause of the statute, to override the considered opinion of parliament as to what is necessary to protect the public treasury with regard to financial commitments. That principle cannot be defended on any other theory than that of ex necessitate. While I am quite willing to admit that in war time the necessity may arise to do this or that by order in council while the house is in recess, and the government might be able to justify it; but when parliament is in session, as it was on the date when this order in council was passed, there is absolutely no justification for legislating by order in council on matters of this kind.
I have not been able to go through all the cases in connection with which this government has acted in this manner, but I have a sample lot here. Some of them are important and others are of no importance at all. But all of them were acted upon while parliament was in session. The last one I have here is dated March 18 and refers to the reserve army regulations, 1941. I do not suppose that it was necessary as a matter of practice to come to parliament to get approval of these reserve army regulations, 1941. That procedure might delay parliament, but the fact

This was passed by virtue of the War Measures Act and "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other act or regulation". I wonder why that provision was not brought before parliament by my hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health. Was he afraid to consult parliament, or was it done so hurriedly as a result of the pressure brought to bear upon him by members of this house on behalf of the 20,000 soldiers who had been set adrift in this country that he acted in defiance of and flouted the will of parliament? He had no authority at all on principle to do this by order in council.
The War Measures Act, Mr. Chairman, under this government has set aside the constitution of this country, and I submit in all fairness that it ought not to be used for all the purposes for which it has been used. I have given two cases. The last one I will not question at all, but the first case I do question.
There is another case which comes in order of sequence that I would not question. Here is P.C. 6645, passed on the recommendation of my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence. I have them all here, but I am not going to take time to read them all. I will just put them on the record. P.C. 6645 was approved on November 19, designating the military forces of Canada as the Canadian Army. This was passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act and "notwithstanding the Militia Act, chapter 132 of the revised statutes of Canada or any other act or law". Aside from the principle involved, I would not raise one word of protest if the government want to change the name of the army. But there is a principle involved, and I submit that the War Measures Act was not set up to cover any of these proceedings.
I wish to call attention to another one, P.C. 6647, approved on the same day, November 19, 1940, containing regulations to govern the air cadet corps. This was passed pursuant

to the War Measures Act and "notwithstanding the provisions of the Militia Act or any other act or law". I assume that it is not an important matter except for the regulations, but it violates the principle just the same.
