This was passed pursuant to the War Measures Act and "notwithstanding the provisions of any other act, law, statute or regulation".
We have even altered the Radio Act and the Canada Shipping Act under the guise of war necessity. P.C. 1014, amending the defence of Canada regulations, was approved on February 22, 1941, when this house, if my memory serves me aright, was in session. This order in council amended regulation 11 of the defence of Canada regulations and provided that "notwithstanding anything contained in the Radio Act, 1938, or in the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, or in any regulation made under such acts, the Minister of Transport might prohibit the use of radio apparatus on any ship within Canadian waters". That probably was necessary, and as a matter of practicability no one would greatly object to it. But it was a violation of the principle just the same.

When I came to look at the date I was surprised to learn that the house was in session at that time.
The hon. gentleman asks why we did not bring it before the House of Commons. Because we had the power to do it this way, abundant power. There was no doubt in the mind of anyone who knew anything about it that what we were doing was a good and wise thing to do; so we went ahead and did it, and got on with our business. I wish to say one word. From what the hon. gentleman has said, I take it that as far as the order in council changing the name of the army was concerned, he will admit that it was perfectly legal in every way under the authority of the War Measures Act.
I would say it did not matter whether it was or not; it was all right to do it. I am thinking principally about the public treasury.

The same, I think, could be said with regard to the matter of claims arising in Iceland. There we provided machinery whereby small claims could, after being considered and approved by a joint committee, be settled by the paymasters of the forces and then reported to national defence headquarters. That was in connection with claims not exceeding $250 with regard to accidents and matters of that kind, which would take literally months if referred to national defence headquarters. Then, after that length of time, when you were through with them, you still would have claims for only $250. In the meantime a situation was arising in Iceland under which the population felt that the Canadian forces were not honouring their obligations. Therefore, with regard to that far-flung territory it was decided to make that provision in order that small claims might be settled by officers expressly authorized in this connection; that is to say, the officer commanding, in cooperation with a joint civilian and army committee established to pass upon these small claims. I do not think my hon. friend will suggest that it would have been worth while

Subject to .the provisions of section three hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of his majesty in the right of Canada, as maybe deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
Then section 5 provides:
Every order or regulation passed under the authority of this act shall be tabled in parliament forthwith if parliament is in session and *a copy thereof sent to every member of the House of Commons and of the Senate and if parliament is not in session then every such order or regulation shall be forthwith published in the Canada Gazette and copies thereof sent to every member of the House of Commons and of the Senate forthwith; provided that any of the steps specified in this section may be omitted o,r deferred if the governor in council considers such omission or deferment necessary in the national interest having regard to the special circumstances.
Those regulations were passed under that statute, not under the War Measures Act. My hon. friend says the War Measures Act was mentioned; I presume that would be for the sake of greater certainty, but those regulations were made under the express authority of the act I have just quoted, and brought down by me, and they have been laid on the table of this house, as the statute required. I say to my hon. friend that I am sorry I cannot get into the frame of mind that he wants me to get into, namely, that of making this committee a confessional, of coming here and saying, "Mea culpa" and bringing myself to the state of penitence which he has commended in referring to my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence for Air. I am not to blame in connection with this matter; the regulations were made under this statute. I stand by them, and I say that my hon. friend can have no objection in the world to them. I say that his point is absolutely ill-founded, that there was complete power under that statute to make these regulations.

Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices-further amount required, $149,500.
Could we have a breakdown of this item? Why is this increase necessary?

There is an increase of $149,500. The main appropriation for 1940-41 was S14,155,190, and the estimated expenditure $14,302,065. This is in the neighbourhood of $158,000 less than for the year 1939-40, but a comparison of the figures does not serve any useful purpose, for the reason that as a measure of economy the department effected certain reductions in
Supply-Post Office

service in 1940-41, such as the non-delivery of mail on Saturday afternoons and statutory holidays. On the other hand, there has been a very large increase in postal revenue during the year. The latest figures show that for the nine months ended December 31, 1940, the gross revenue increased by $2,739,313 over the corresponding period of the previous year. This augmented income involves a corresponding increase in the volume of mail, the handling of which necessitates increased staff and expenditure not only for salaries but for conveyance of the mail by railway and in other ways.
What is the estimated saving for the ensuing year from the doing away of the Saturday afternoon mail delivery?
It is a substantial sum running into several hundred thousands of dollars, but I would prefer the hon. member to raise that question on the main estimates.

Have there been any complaints about the pilfering of packages sent through the post to our soldiers in the old country? I refer more particularly to cigarettes and small luxuries for the soldiers. I \ave had reports that there is much pilfering going on.

Early last spring and in the early part of last summer there were a great many complaints from people who had sent parcels, and there were also a considerable number of complaints in the press. Since then, a wholly new system has been inaugurated for handling cigarettes and tobacco parcels for the troops overseas. Most of the cigarette and tobacco parcels are sent through the four large tobacco companies, which now list these parcels. Under the supervision of post office officials they are cleared through customs, brought to the base post office and given unit sortation, and the bags are then sealed. Therefore these parcels are now receiving dentically the same treatment as registered mail. There has been a great improvement, and only a very small fraction of the number of complaints that were received some time ago are now received.
An assistant of Mr. Fortier, the chief inspector, is at the base post office at Ottawa in charge, with assistants, of making investigations into all complaints received. At the present time we know the dispatch number, the train the parcel goes on and the ship, and the contents of the respective bags. Most of these cigarettes and tobacco parcels go through the four large tobacco companies. A list of the contents of the bag is sent overseas.
[Mr. Mulock.l
I hope hon. members will not ask for further details because we do not want to give too much detail. I can assure hon. members, however, that a close check is being made on these parcels. I might add that all the employees in the postal corps overseas are former employees of the Post Office Department, and there has been no case of any employee of the Post Office Department or of the postal corps overseas having been guilty of any irregularity in the handling of cigarette and tobacco parcels.
Was it discovered why parcels were going astray?

I shall be glad to explain some of the troubles. At the beginning of the war it was found that as high as 10 and 15 per cent of the letters and parcels addressed to the soldiers were being improperly addressed, and it was taking a large staff to correct the addresses. In some instances this was impossible on account of lack of identification. That has been improved considerably, because we have sent out approximately
150,000	notices to the dependents of the men serving overseas, giving detailed instructions and examples of how parcels should be addressed. The press of this country, particularly the press gallery, were extremely helpful in that matter. The press gallery went down to the base post office and saw how the mails were handled, and then they assisted in bringing home to the public the proper way to address the mail. They saw examples before them of improper addressing.

Generally speaking, is the enrolment increasing or decreasing at these residential schools?

The tendency is towards an increase. That touches another question which has to do with general Indian welfare. There is no doubt that improvements in recent years in the medical care of Indians, and in supplying them with those necessaries of life which perhaps they lacked before, have tended to bring about an increase in the Indian population, and as the population increases, the number of children for whom school facilities have to be provided also increases. It is estimated that the Indian population is increasing at the rate of one and a half or two per cent a year.

The Indians at Burleigh Falls are squatting on government land, the canal property, and the children have no school to go to. There are about seventeen children. These Indians are not paying taxes to anyone and the government refuses to recognize them. The Children's Aid Society of Peterborough have written to me with regard to them. There should be a school for these children. The Indian Affairs branch contend they are not Indians but half-breeds, although on the registration cards they are put down as Indians. The township will not take responsibility for them. Is there any chance of the departihent looking into the matter with a
view to making a small grant? I know the province or perhaps the county would help. At present the school inspector goes there once a week and holds school in the dining room of a little store, but these children need education.

If they are, we must decline responsibility for them. If we accepted responsibility for half-breeds, it would land us in a sea of troubles. Consequently, they are the responsibility not of the Indian Affairs branch, but of the province.

In the district from which I come there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction regarding inspection. 433. Industrial Disputes Investigation Act- further amount required, $20,000.

Before this item carries, I wish to draw attention to what I consider to be a vicious and pernicious principle which has entered into the matter of conciliations in labour disputes. I would not take the time to place it before the committee to-night were it not for the fact that I have in mind a board decision which has not been satisfactory to the employees concerned, who at the present time are on strike. It does not follow that I think all decisions should be in favour of the employees. That is a chance they must take in accepting the principle of conciliation, a principle which I believe to be a very good one. What I am objecting to now is the principle laid down in section 10 of order in council P.C. 7440. The section reads as follows:
In the case of any dispute in which a contract with a government department is involved, the board of conciliation and investigation to which the dispute is submitted shall afford to the department concerned the privilege of submitting to the board a brief in writing as to the views of the department on any matter touching the dispute.
The way in which that works is this. A dispute develops with regard to wages and working conditions, or any matter which affects employees, in a certain *work in which the government is concerned. Either side makes application to the Department of Labour for a board. In the course of time a board is granted, and then another department of the government, the same government which has granted the application for the board, and has appointed the chairman of the board, sends its representative to appear before the board-

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member means "the chairman"; he means the representative of the employer.

Yes, that is right. But I am pointing out that the government appoints the board; it may appoint the chairman, and then .a representative of the government appears before this board. The minister shakes his head, but I happen to have under my hand proof that this takes place. The representative appears before the board. This order in council says that he shall place the representations of the department concerned in writing. That is bad enough; as a matter of fact, it should not be done.
The case I have under my hand is that of a board which was granted in a dispute between
H.	F. McLean, Limited, and its plumbers, steam-fitters, sprinkler-fitters and general pipefitters employed at He de Salaberry, Quebec, members of local 144, United Association of Journeymen Plumbers and Steam Fitters. I am reading from a copy of the majority findings and the minority findings of the board, with a covering letter signed by the assistant deputy minister of labour and registrar.
In this case, H. B. Chase, director general of labour relations in the Department of Munitions and Supply, made, according to section 10 of order in council P.C. 7440, a submission to the conciliation board, and he not only made the submission in writing, but, according to the minority report appeared and made argument before the board. I shall show, before I have finished, that he went so far as to point out to the board that it would be illegal under order in council P.C. 7440 for the board to grant an increase of wages in the case. The minority report in the dispute is signed by the representative of the employees. I quote:
In accordance with clause 10 of order in council P.C. 7440, dated December 16, 1940, Mr. Howard Chase submitted a brief in writing on behalf of the Department of Munitions and Supply of the Dominion of Canada. Not only did Mr. Chase submit his brief, as provided for in section 10 of order in council P.C. 7440, but he furthermore read it, added comments, made comparisons and even touched the legal aspect of the fair wages policy of the government of Canada, together with possible legal rights being derived from a collective labour agreement, now in force in the district of Montreal.
That statement from the employees' representative bears out the point I made. The government sets up a board, appoints a chairman, and another government department appears before the board and declares that the board cannot make a certain award because it would be illegal according to order in council P.C. 7440. It seems to me that such pro* cedure reduces the conciliation boards, in any industry in which the government is concerned, to a farce. They cannot in the circumstances be of the slightest value whatever. As a matter of fact, any one who reads the submission made by Mr. Chase to the board and then reads the majority findings of the board and compares the two, will find that the majority findings carry out every suggestion made by Mr. Chase. Let me read two sections on page 4:
The attention of your board is directed to order in council P.C. 7440, which has at least an indirect bearing on the case before you. It is true that the request is for an allowance for board and transportation expenses and it is equally true that an allowance for board is equivalent to an increase in wages.
With regard to sprinkler-fitters, the provincial decree above referred to specifies that when employed outside of the city of Montreal they will receive an extra 20 cents per hour. It is not referred to as an allowance for board-it

216S
Supply-Labour-Industrial Disputes
is a flat increase in the wage rate. Therefore, in the present instance while the request of the applicants is for an allowance for board, it is in effect a request for an increase in the wage rates, and as such, falls within the terms of P.C. 7440.
It seems to me it would be better, instead of stringing the employees along, to use the language of the street, and allowing them to think that they will get something in this way, for the Department of Labour or the Department of Munitions and Supply, or both, to tell the representatives of these labour organizations that there is no use in their applying for a board, that under order in council P.C. 7440 it is illegal for a board to give an increase in wages. It is an amazing fact. I have brought to the attention of this house several times during the last twelve months the lack of labour representation on the war boards apart from the national labour supply council. This is the only war board set up on which there was a representative of labour, and we find that this representative is used by the government to beat down the wages and impair the conditions of employees instead of helping them. I submit to the Minister of Labour that he give this matter careful consideration. It is, as I said before, nothing more than a farce to have a condition of affairs such as this. If it continues sooner or later labour will become so exasperated that not only a small number of workers as in this case, but a large number, will be involved in labour disputes and may to a very great extent interfere with war production.

I do not think I shall require many minutes to reply to the remarks of the hon. member. I quite agree with him that the reason why section 10 of the order in council was put in was to obviate the very thing that happened at Valleyfield. There is no question about it. The labour supply council went into the matter thoroughly, and it was their idea that putting that clause in, and allowing a memorandum to be submitted to the board by any interested department, was the farthest that the government should go. That condition was not observed in Valleyfield. I did not know of it at the time the board was sitting. Had an application been made for a rehearing, it might have been necessary to grant it, but no such application was made. I can assure the hon. member that the situation will not recur, because it is not in accordance with the section of the order in council.

This is not the first instance in which the activities of Mr. Chase have been drawn to my attention. When the
(Mr. Maclnnis.]
application of the employees of National Steel Car Corporation was before the Department of Labour for a board, Mr. Chase was sent, either by the Department of Labour or by the Department of Munitions and Supply, to Hamilton. The men understood that he had the granting of the request for a board with him. When he got to Hamilton, however, he told the employees that they could not get a board, and that even if they did, they could not get an award because of order in council P.C. 7440. That is the information I have from representatives of the employees of the National Steel Car Corporation. If the minister has information on the discussions which took place at the trades and labour congress at Vancouver last September, he will know as well as I do the statements that were made there with regard to Mr. Chase's activities respecting wages in the shipyards. I think it is time the Department of Labour told Mr. Chase where he gets off at.

I can assure the hon. member that Mr. Chase was not sent to Hamilton by the Department of Labour. I do not know what representations he made, but if he made a representation that they should not have a board he w'as certainly mistaken, because they have a board. I do not know what representations he made in Hamilton, nor do I know the purpose of his visit. Certainly I can assure the hon. member that he was not sent by the Department of Labour.

May I ask the minister who Mr. Chase is, where he comes from, how he came to get into the department as a representative of labour, and who recommended him? His activities have not been in the best interests of organized labour.

I can hardly be expected to say who recommended Mr. Chase for that department. It is not a department over which I have any jurisdiction whatever. I believe he was a member of one of the railroad brotherhoods.
The locomotive engineers.

I was not sure, but one of those. When the war supply board was originally set up, he came to Ottawa, I believe, and while he was not a member of the board he was active in labour relations. What his antecedents are, or the recommendations that were made respecting him, I do not know.

He was not recommended to the government by organized labour as its representative. That, I think, is the point which is being made.
